items.title: Climate talks fail
items.source: BBC Learning English from the News (text)
items.summary: The COP31 talks held in Turkey were the latest in a yearly conference between UN nations to plan and agree commitments and action on climate change. This was the longest climate conference ever, but the talks collapsed on Sunday after countries were unable to reach an agreement. Many countries, including EU countries and Pacific island nations were unhappy because the draft agreement didn’t include the term ‘fossil fuels’. Another disagreement was over payments to poorer countries to help them to adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures. Many of these countries wanted the agreement to say exactly how much financial help richer countries would commit to. Get a free worksheet for this episode here: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/learning-english-from-the-news_2026/261125
items.body: COP31 climate conference ends without agreement. Many countries were unhappy because the draft agreement didn’t include the term ‘fossil fuels’. The COP31 talks held in Turkey were the latest in a yearly conference between UN nations to plan and agree commitments and action on climate change.

items.summary: The Army is set to destroy thousands of pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa after several delays, as residents prepare for the potential spread of toxic lead dust. Lawmakers in both parties are pressing for answers about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s national security scandal and considering tighter restrictions on chip sales to China.

items.title: Want a better winter workout? Train your muscle clocks
items.summary: TikTok has another trend: the winter arc. It’s a self-improvement challenge where people try to be their best self in the 3 months leading up to New Year – often, through exercise. We at Short Wave wanted to know if the science really holds up: Is ramping up your exercise routine when your circadian rhythm may be struggling with less light really a good idea? So we called up NPR health correspondent, Will Stone . He’s done a deep dive on what scientists do and don’t know about exercise and our circadian rhythms. To read more of Will’s reporting on creating a solid exercise routine . If you liked this episode, check out our episodes on “circadian depression” , and the science of jet lag and how to avoid it. Interested in more health science? Email us your question at shortwave@npr.org .

items.title: Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast
items.summary: Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, the US Coast Guard said.

items.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
items.summary: Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one hostage-taker was killed. Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.

items.title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants
items.summary: DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 1th Amendment to the US constitution , which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment , and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants. The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th specifically established birthright citizenship, due process and equal rights for all races under the law, and furthermore barred insurrectionists from holding public office, all of which Trump appears casually intent on vandalising, airily amnesiac about his oath to uphold the constitution.

items.title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
items.summary: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role.

items.title: Tidal bans 100% AI-generated music with plans to delete more than 27m tracks
items.summary: Streaming service says 43% of uploads to platform in past 90 days were made entirely by artificial intelligence The music streaming service Tidal has announced it will ban entirely AI-generated music from its platform and remove millions of songs, saying AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans”. “To ensure Tidal remains the best place for artists to share their work, and for listeners to enjoy it, we’re removing all tracks that we determine are 100% AI generated,” the company announced on Tuesday.

items.title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
items.summary: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation. Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.
items.body: China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

items.body:
2023 — Three Palestinian students are injured in a shooting in Burlington, Vermont.

2021 — A fire at a coal mine in Kemerovo Oblast kills 51 people.

2009 — Jeddah floods: Freak rains swamp the city of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, during an ongoing Hajj pilgrimage. Three thousand cars are swept away and 122 people perish in the torrents, with 350 others missing.

2008 — Cyclone Nisha strikes northern Sri Lanka, killing 15 people and displacing 90,000 others while dealing the region the highest rainfall in nine decades.

2000 — The 2000 Baku earthquake, with a Richter magnitude of 7.0 kills 26 people in Baku, Azerbaijan.
